cases.title: Why Slack and Microsoft Teams diverged on threaded replies
cases.prompt: In Slack, most messages post directly to the channel and threading a reply is optional; in Microsoft Teams, every new channel post starts its own thread and every reply is nested under it by default. Why might these two workplace messaging products have made opposite defaults for how conversations are structured, and which default would you choose for a new team-communication product?
context: Slack launched in 2013 as a real-time messaging app for teams, with channel-first messaging and an opt-in threading feature added later.
Microsoft Teams launched in 2017 as part of Microsoft 365, with every channel post structured as the start of its own thread that replies nest under.
Salesforce acquired Slack in 2021; Microsoft Teams ships bundled with Microsoft 365 and integrates with Outlook, SharePoint, and OneDrive.
assumptions: assumed: comparing the default channel-posting behaviour only, not direct messages, since DMs are largely undifferentiated between the two products
assumed: the interviewer wants a recommendation for a new team-communication product being designed today, not a retrofit of either existing app
followUps: How would your recommendation change for a 5-person startup versus a 5,000-person enterprise?
Teams' thread-per-post model can produce dozens of parallel threads in a busy channel. How would you mitigate that?
How would you measure whether your chosen default is actually reducing confusion versus just feeling different?

stages.walkthrough: I'll scope this to the default behaviour for new posts inside a shared channel, not direct messages, since DMs are largely undifferentiated between the two products. I'll assume the interviewer wants a recommendation for a new team-communication product being designed today, informed by what Slack and Teams chose, not a retrofit of either existing app. My plan: connect each product's mission to its threading default, segment each product's core users, identify the specific problem each default solves, then recommend a default for a new product.

Slack's mission is replacing email with fast, ambient, flowing conversation -- its channel-first, thread-optional model is built for teams that want an idea to reach the room the instant someone has it, with threading as an escape hatch for side conversations rather than the norm. Microsoft Teams' mission is extending Microsoft 365's structured collaboration -- meetings, documents, calendars -- into chat, for organizations that already run on Outlook and SharePoint and need conversations to be traceable back to a specific topic. Slack optimizes for velocity of ideas; Teams optimizes for auditability of decisions. That difference in what each company is fundamentally trying to be the 'operating layer' for explains why one treats structure as optional and the other as mandatory.

Slack's core segment is flat, fast-moving teams -- startups, product and engineering groups -- who value low friction over long-term traceability, since their channels are small enough that a scroll-back usually finds what's needed. Teams' core segment is large enterprises with governance and compliance needs, where a channel might have hundreds of members and a manager needs to know exactly which reply belongs to which original topic months later. These segments are mutually exclusive in what they need from structure: the Slack segment experiences mandatory threading as friction, while the Teams segment experiences a flat channel as noise they can't navigate.

For the Slack-style user, the journey moment is 'I have a quick, half-formed thought and want it in the channel before I lose momentum' -- any required step (choosing a thread, or starting one) is friction against that goal, so the problem is minimizing steps between having a thought and it being visible to the team. For the Teams-style user, the journey moment is 'I need to find out who said what about a specific proposal three weeks ago' in a channel with dozens of daily posts -- the problem is that a flat, undifferentiated stream makes a specific conversation impossible to isolate. Both are real problems, not just preferences, because each is tied to a concrete failure: lost momentum on one side, lost accountability on the other. This ties back to mission: Slack's ambient-conversation promise breaks if posting feels like paperwork, while Teams' auditability promise breaks if a decision can't be traced.

Three directions for a new product: copy Slack's opt-in model, copy Teams' mandatory-thread model, or a hybrid where every post starts flat but automatically gets promoted into a visible thread once it collects two or more replies, so structure emerges only where a real sub-conversation exists. On an impact x effort grid, the hybrid is more effort to build well but avoids forcing either segment into the other's friction, so I'd choose it for a general-purpose new product; if I knew my target segment was one of the two extremes, I'd just copy that product's default outright rather than build something more complex. The key risk with the hybrid is inconsistency -- users won't develop a stable mental model of where a reply will land -- mitigated by making the promotion threshold visible and predictable rather than silent. This choice serves a mission of letting structure follow actual conversation shape rather than imposing one philosophy on every team regardless of size or need.

pitfalls: Declaring one product's default 'better' without naming which segment's problem it actually solves
Ignoring that Teams' default is inseparable from its Microsoft 365 distribution advantage, which is a business reason as much as a UX one

cases.title: Why Netflix and YouTube designed autoplay to serve two different goals
cases.prompt: Netflix autoplays the next episode of the show you're already watching; YouTube autoplays a next video chosen by its recommendation algorithm, which may have nothing to do with what you just watched. Why might these two video platforms have built such different autoplay logic, and which approach would you choose for a new video product?
context: Netflix introduced 'Post-Play', which automatically begins the next episode in a series after the current one ends, in 2012, later adding a user-facing toggle to disable it.
YouTube's autoplay queues and plays a next video chosen by its recommendation system once the current video ends, and has offered a toggle to disable this for many years.
Netflix is a subscription-only streaming service with a fixed monthly fee; YouTube's core business is advertising against watch time, supplemented by YouTube Premium subscriptions.
assumptions: assumed: comparing autoplay-after-a-video-ends behaviour only, not Netflix's separate autoplay-preview-on-hover feature
assumed: the interviewer wants a recommendation for a new video product being designed today
followUps: How would your answer change for a video product that has no serialized content at all?
What's the risk of algorithmic cross-content autoplay pulling users toward content that erodes trust over time?
How would you measure whether your chosen autoplay model is helping retention rather than just increasing session length?

stages.walkthrough: I'll scope this to autoplay-after-a-video-ends behaviour only, not Netflix's separate hover-preview autoplay feature, and assume the interviewer wants a recommendation for a new video product being designed today. My plan: connect each product's autoplay logic to its mission, segment the viewers each serves, identify the specific problem each autoplay model solves, then recommend an approach for a new product.

Netflix's mission is delivering satisfying, binge-worthy storytelling, and its revenue comes from flat subscription retention rather than ad impressions, so autoplaying the next episode serves the story a user already chose without any incentive to pull them toward unrelated content. YouTube's mission is being the place people go for any video and maximizing time spent across its whole library, and its revenue is tied directly to ad impressions and watch time, so autoplay is a discovery and retention mechanism across the entire catalog, not fidelity to one series. That difference in business model -- flat subscription versus watch-time-driven advertising -- is the seed of the divergent autoplay logic.

Netflix's relevant segment is a viewer already committed to a specific show; the value autoplay adds is removing the tiny friction between episodes for someone already engaged with that narrative. YouTube's relevant segment spans viewers who just finished a standalone video with no built-in 'next' like an episode would have, and often no further intent at all -- YouTube's job is to manufacture a next intent, since a large share of its catalog is standalone rather than serialized. These segments need fundamentally different things from autoplay: one wants continuation of a chosen story, the other needs a reason to keep watching at all.

Netflix's persona finishes an episode and wants to keep going, but the short decision window before an active click is a danger point where they close the app instead of continuing a story they were already invested in -- the problem is a brief gap killing momentum on a choice already made. YouTube's persona finishes a standalone video with no default next intent -- the problem is different: with nothing else queued, watch time simply ends unless something proposes a next video, so YouTube's problem is discovery, not momentum-preservation. Both are real problems tied to a specific loss (lost momentum versus lost session), and both connect to mission: Netflix's binge-worthy promise depends on continuation feeling effortless, while YouTube's 'anything, anytime' promise depends on there always being a next reason to stay.

Options for a new product: same-series-only autoplay (Netflix's model), algorithmic cross-content autoplay (YouTube's model), or a hybrid that defaults to series-continuation when a user is inside a series and falls back to algorithmic recommendation otherwise. For a general-purpose video product carrying both serialized and standalone content, I'd choose the hybrid, since it serves both problems identified above without forcing one philosophy onto content it doesn't fit. The main risk with the algorithmic half is content drift eroding user trust by pulling attention somewhere unintended; the mitigation is an easy, always-visible way to pause or disable autoplay, plus capping how far a recommendation can drift from the original topic before it's offered. This serves the mission of respecting the viewer's actual intent -- continuing a story when there is one, proposing a new one when there isn't -- rather than optimizing for session length regardless of what the viewer came for.

pitfalls: Assuming YouTube's algorithmic autoplay is 'worse' just because it wanders off-topic, when off-topic discovery is exactly its job
Ignoring that Netflix's flat-subscription business model removes any incentive to maximize minutes the way YouTube's ad-driven model does

cases.title: Why Zomato Gold and Swiggy One took different shapes as subscription programs
cases.prompt: Zomato Gold is built around dine-out perks and discounts at partner restaurants, while Swiggy One bundles free delivery and benefits across Swiggy's own family of services (food delivery, Instamart, Dineout, Genie). Why might India's two largest food-delivery platforms have designed such differently-shaped subscription programs, and which shape would you choose for a new food-delivery entrant?
context: Zomato launched its Gold membership programme in December 2017, initially centered on dine-out benefits at partner restaurants.
Swiggy launched Swiggy One in 2023 as a unified membership spanning food delivery, its Instamart quick-commerce vertical, Dineout, and its Genie pickup-and-drop service.
Zomato and Swiggy are the two largest food-delivery platforms in India and compete directly across delivery, dining, and quick-commerce.
assumptions: assumed: comparing each programme's core positioning as originally launched, not every subsequent iteration or rebrand
assumed: the interviewer wants a recommendation for a new food-delivery entrant building a subscription programme from scratch
followUps: How would your recommendation change for an entrant that only operates a single delivery vertical, with no dine-out or quick-commerce business?
What's the risk of a new entrant copying a bundled membership shape before it actually operates the services being bundled?
How would you decide when it's time to evolve a subscription programme's shape as the company adds new verticals?

stages.walkthrough: I'll compare each programme's core positioning as originally launched, not every later iteration or rebrand, and assume the interviewer wants a recommendation for a new food-delivery entrant designing a subscription programme from scratch. My plan: connect each programme to its parent company's mission and history, segment the users each shape serves, identify the underlying problem each solves, then recommend a shape for a new entrant.

Zomato's historical strength is discovery and dine-out -- it grew as a restaurant-discovery and reviews product before it grew as a delivery business, so a membership anchored in restaurant partnerships plays directly to that legacy and its deep restaurant relationships. Swiggy grew delivery-first and diversified into adjacent instant-need services like grocery and pickup, so a membership that bundles value across its own multi-service portfolio plays to its strategy of making a single Swiggy account cover everything a household needs same-day. Each programme's shape is less a pure UX choice than a reflection of what each company's underlying business already is.

Zomato's natural segment for a dine-out-anchored programme is the going-out diner who eats at restaurants regularly and cares about a visible discount at the table. Swiggy's natural segment for a bundled programme is the at-home household user who already orders food, groceries, and occasional errands through Swiggy's various services and wants one saved fee to cover free delivery everywhere, rather than a restaurant discount. These are different value propositions serving different moments -- one at the restaurant table, one at home ordering in -- and are mutually exclusive since a diner focused on eating out doesn't especially value delivery-fee waivers across services they don't use.

For the Zomato-style diner, the problem is that eating out is expensive per-visit, and a loyalty mechanism needs to reduce that per-visit cost visibly enough to change where they choose to eat -- the journey stage is picking a restaurant, where a visible discount changes behaviour. For the Swiggy-style household, the problem is delivery fees accumulating quietly across many small, frequent orders across different Swiggy services -- the journey stage is checkout, repeated many times a week, where a flat membership fee removes a recurring annoyance rather than driving one big decision. Both are real problems tied to a specific moment of friction, and each connects back to what its company is trying to be the default for -- dining decisions in Zomato's case, everyday household ordering in Swiggy's.

Options for a new entrant: a dine-out-anchored membership, a delivery-fee-waiver membership, or a bundled-across-services membership. On an impact x effort grid, the real constraint isn't user preference alone but which services the entrant actually operates -- a delivery-only entrant with no dine-out inventory or second vertical can only credibly build the delivery-fee-waiver model, since it has nothing else to bundle. The lesson is that subscription shape should follow the company's actual value chain rather than copying a competitor's shape wholesale; the risk of copying a bundled shape without owning multiple verticals is promising cross-service value with nothing behind it, which erodes trust in the membership itself. For V1, I'd match the programme's shape tightly to whatever the entrant's core existing service already is, and treat expansion into a bundled model as something to earn only once a second vertical genuinely exists.

pitfalls: Declaring one subscription design 'better' without noting that each is downstream of what verticals the company actually operates, not just user research
Recommending a new entrant copy a bundled multi-service membership shape before it operates more than one service

cases.title: Why Uber and Ola diverged on how visible surge pricing is to riders
cases.prompt: Uber shows riders an explicit surge multiplier (for example, '1.8x') before they confirm a ride during high demand, alongside an upfront total fare; Ola typically shows only the upfront estimated fare, without prominently exposing a comparable multiplier. Why might these two ride-hailing platforms have made different calls on how transparent to be about surge pricing, and which approach would you choose for a new ride-hailing entrant?
context: Uber pioneered surge pricing (dynamic pricing that rises during periods of high demand) and has displayed a visible multiplier alongside an upfront fare quote in its rider app for many years.
Ola operates primarily in India and other select markets, and presents riders with an upfront estimated fare at booking without prominently surfacing an equivalent multiplier figure.
Both companies have faced public criticism and regulatory scrutiny in various markets over surge or dynamic pricing, including during emergencies or extreme weather.
assumptions: assumed: comparing the rider-facing booking screen only, not driver-side earnings transparency, which is a separate question
assumed: the interviewer wants a recommendation for a new ride-hailing entrant building its pricing UI from scratch
followUps: How would your recommendation change in a market with strict regulatory limits on dynamic pricing during emergencies?
What's the risk of showing a raw multiplier to a first-time or infrequent rider unfamiliar with the concept?
How would you A/B test whether visible surge pricing actually changes booking behaviour versus just changing perception?

stages.walkthrough: I'll scope this to the rider-facing booking screen only, not driver-side earnings transparency, and assume the interviewer wants a recommendation for a new ride-hailing entrant designing its pricing UI from scratch. My plan: connect each company's mission to its pricing-transparency choice, segment the riders each choice serves, identify the specific problem each solves, then recommend an approach and its mitigations.

Uber built its brand globally partly on the promise of algorithmic, marketplace-style fairness, and showing the multiplier is a transparency mechanic meant to make demand-based pricing feel like an explainable market mechanism rather than an arbitrary price hike, reinforcing trust in markets where Uber competes on being the more legible choice. Ola's mission has leaned toward being the accessible, mass-market option across a wide range of Indian cities and price-sensitive riders, where a single, simple upfront number may cause less anxiety or perceived unfairness than a fluctuating multiplier that can look punitive to a price-sensitive audience. Each company's transparency choice reflects a different bet on what builds trust with its specific rider base.

A segment that benefits from seeing the multiplier is the price-sensitive-but-analytical rider who wants to understand and potentially wait out a price spike, using visible surge as a signal to delay their trip. A segment better served by a single upfront number is the rider who wants a fast decision with no extra cognitive step, where an unfamiliar-looking multiplier adds confusion without adding information they'll actually act on. These segments want fundamentally different things from a price display: one wants a lever they can use, the other wants the least friction to a yes-or-no decision, making them mutually exclusive in what 'good' pricing UI looks like.

For the analytical rider, the journey moment is opening the app during a demand spike and deciding whether to book now or wait; without a visible multiplier, they can't judge whether prices are temporarily elevated or just normal today, so the problem is an inability to make an informed wait-or-book decision. For the friction-averse rider, the same screen produces the opposite problem: an unfamiliar multiplier next to a currency amount can read as confusing or alarming, especially for a first-time or infrequent user, making a two-number display a bigger hesitation point than a single upfront total. Both problems are real and tied to a specific negative outcome -- a missed opportunity to save money on one side, booking hesitation or distrust on the other -- and both connect to how each company wants to be perceived under pricing scrutiny.

Options for a new entrant: always show the multiplier, always hide it behind a single upfront fare, or show it conditionally, for example only above a certain surge threshold. Given the regulatory scrutiny dynamic pricing has attracted globally, I'd lean toward showing the multiplier by default since it's the more defensible, transparent choice under scrutiny, even where it isn't the friction-minimizing choice for every rider; V1 would pair a visible multiplier with a plain-language one-line explanation of why it's elevated, serving both trust and comprehension at once. The key risk of visible surge is rider frustration at what can feel like an arbitrary number, mitigated by capping surge during clearly flagged emergency conditions and being explicit that the multiplier reflects real-time driver supply rather than a company decision to raise prices. This serves a mission of earning trust through legibility, even at the cost of some friction for riders who'd prefer not to think about it.

pitfalls: Assuming hiding the multiplier is simply 'less transparent' and therefore worse, without accounting for the confusion a raw multiplier can cause a price-sensitive, infrequent rider
Treating this as a UI-only decision when it's inseparable from each company's regulatory exposure and brand positioning in a given market

cases.title: Why Spotify leaned into algorithmic discovery while Apple Music leaned on human curation
cases.prompt: Spotify built its discovery experience around algorithmically generated, personalized playlists like Discover Weekly; Apple Music has historically leaned more on human-curated editorial playlists and radio programming. Why might these two music-streaming platforms have made different bets on algorithmic versus human-curated discovery, and which approach would you choose for a new music-streaming entrant?
context: Spotify launched Discover Weekly, a personalized algorithmically-generated playlist refreshed every Monday, in 2015, and later added Daily Mix and an annual personalized 'Wrapped' recap.
Apple Music launched in 2015 with a strong emphasis on human-curated editorial playlists and live radio programming, including its Apple Music radio stations.

Spotify's core business began as a pure music-streaming subscription and later diversified into podcasts and audiobooks; Apple Music is offered as part of Apple's broader hardware and services ecosystem, including bundles like Apple One.
assumptions: assumed: comparing each product's discovery-surface emphasis as it shaped up over its first several years, not every feature either has added more recently
assumed: the interviewer wants a recommendation for a new music-streaming entrant building its discovery strategy from scratch
followUps: How would your recommendation change once the entrant has accumulated a few years of listening data?
What's the risk of an entrant trying to out-algorithm an incumbent that has a decade of cross-user listening data?
How would you measure whether editorial curation is actually driving discovery, versus just feeling premium?

stages.walkthrough: I'll compare each product's discovery-surface emphasis as it shaped up over its first several years, not every feature either has added more recently, and assume the interviewer wants a recommendation for a new music-streaming entrant designing its discovery strategy from scratch. My plan: connect each company's mission to its discovery bet, segment the listeners each approach serves, identify the specific problem each solves, then recommend an approach for a new entrant.

Spotify's business is the subscription itself -- its mission is to be the place people spend the most listening hours, so anything that keeps a user engaged and returning, like a weekly personalized drop they look forward to, directly serves retention and justified deep investment in recommendation algorithms trained on a massive cross-user listening dataset. Apple Music is one piece of a broader hardware-and-services ecosystem where the music app's job is partly to make owning Apple devices feel more valuable -- editorial curation lets Apple lean on its long-standing brand association with taste and design, differentiating on human expertise rather than competing purely on algorithmic sophistication against a company with a much larger listening dataset to train on.

Spotify's core segment is the exploratory listener who wants to be surprised by something adjacent to their taste every week and trusts a system that's clearly learning from their behaviour over time. Apple Music's discovery bet serves a listener who trusts editorial authority and cultural context -- fans who want to know why a playlist was made and by whom, not just that an algorithm inferred they'd like it. These are different relationships to discovery: one wants personalization at scale, the other wants curated meaning, making the two segments mutually exclusive in what satisfies them.

For Spotify's exploratory listener, the problem is that manually finding new music matching an evolving taste is time-consuming, and most human curation isn't personalized enough to them specifically -- a weekly algorithmic drop solves 'I want something new that's actually for me' at almost zero effort. For Apple Music's editorial-trusting listener, the problem is that pure algorithmic recommendations can feel repetitive or soulless, recommending more of the same rather than surfacing genuinely new cultural context -- their problem is 'I want to discover through someone whose taste I respect,' which an algorithm alone doesn't satisfy. Both are real problems, not just preferences, and each connects to what its company is actually equipped to deliver -- Spotify's data scale versus Apple's brand and editorial resources.

For a new entrant, options are algorithm-first, which requires significant listening data to train on and is hard to bootstrap with a small user base, editorial-first, which requires an ongoing curation-team cost but works from day one with zero listening data, or a hybrid that starts editorial and layers in personalization as data accumulates. Given a new entrant likely lacks an incumbent's years of cross-user training data, I'd start editorial-first for V1 to deliver quality discovery immediately, then progressively introduce lightweight personalization, such as reordering an editorial playlist based on a listener's own skip behaviour, as data accumulates, rather than attempting to out-algorithm an incumbent on day one. The risk of starting editorial-only is a perceived staleness once competitors' personalization outpaces it; mitigation is being transparent that personalization is a stated near-term roadmap item, not a permanent limitation. This serves a mission of delivering real discovery value immediately, using whatever asset -- data or editorial credibility -- the entrant can actually field on day one.

pitfalls: Assuming algorithmic discovery is strictly more advanced and therefore the right default for any new entrant, ignoring that it requires data an entrant doesn't have
Treating this as a taste question about which produces better playlists rather than a strategic one tied to each company's underlying data and brand assets

cases.title: Why Stripe and Razorpay diverged on how much KYC a merchant clears before going live
cases.prompt: Stripe lets many merchants integrate and start testing payments within minutes of signing up, with full KYC required before real payouts begin; Razorpay requires Indian merchants to submit and clear a heavier set of verification documents, such as business registration, PAN, GST, and bank proof, before going live at all. Why might these two payments platforms have designed such different onboarding sequences, and which sequence would you choose for a new payments product?
context: Stripe operates across many countries and is widely known for a self-serve, developer-first signup flow that lets merchants begin integrating and testing in a sandbox almost immediately.

Razorpay operates primarily in India and, as a Reserve Bank of India-regulated payment aggregator, requires merchants to complete business and bank verification, such as PAN, GST, and company registration documents, before processing live transactions.

India's payment aggregators have operated under RBI guidelines, in effect since 2020, that mandate specific merchant due-diligence and KYC standards before an aggregator can process live payments on a merchant's behalf.
assumptions: assumed: comparing the sequence and timing of KYC relative to when a merchant can start integrating, not the total documentation eventually required by either
assumed: the interviewer wants a recommendation for a new payments product being designed today, informed by both models
followUps: How would your sequencing recommendation change for a market with no equivalent regulatory KYC mandate at all?
What's the risk of a payments platform over-complying with KYC requirements beyond what its regulator actually mandates?
How would you design the sandbox experience so a developer gets real signal before committing to the KYC process?

stages.walkthrough: I'll compare the sequence and timing of KYC relative to when a merchant can start integrating, not the total documentation eventually required by either, and assume the interviewer wants a recommendation for a new payments product informed by both models. My plan: connect each company's mission to its onboarding sequence, segment the merchants each serves, identify the specific problem each sequence solves, then recommend a sequence for a new entrant.

Stripe's mission has centered on removing friction for developers to start building, making it as easy as possible to write the first line of payment-integration code, so a sandbox-first, KYC-deferred flow serves that mission directly by letting a developer validate the integration works before committing to paperwork. Razorpay operates under direct regulatory obligation from the RBI as a licensed payment aggregator in India, where the law itself requires merchant due diligence to be substantially complete before live payment processing, meaning Razorpay's sequencing isn't purely a product choice but a compliance floor set by its regulator.

Stripe's segment spans many regulatory regimes with varying requirements, and a meaningful share of its users are individual developers or small teams prototyping before they've even decided to launch a real business -- for them, a fast sandbox start with deferred KYC matches how exploratory their intent often is. Razorpay's segment is Indian businesses in a single, more uniformly regulated market, most of whom are onboarding specifically because they're already operating a registered business and intend to go live, not experimenting speculatively -- for them, front-loading verification doesn't cost as much in lost exploratory momentum since going live is already their clear intent.

For Stripe's exploratory developer, the problem is that requiring full business verification before any integration testing would kill a large share of prototyping-stage signups who haven't yet committed to launching -- the journey moment is wanting to see if the integration even works technically before deciding it's worth the paperwork. For Razorpay's Indian merchant, the problem is different: the platform itself carries regulatory liability for processing payments through an insufficiently verified merchant, so the risk being managed is the platform's own compliance exposure and its downstream users' fraud risk, not user drop-off. These are different problems because one is about preserving developer momentum, the other is about a hard regulatory floor Razorpay cannot design around.

For a new payments product, the sequencing choice is largely determined by the regulatory environment it will operate in, not by user-experience preference alone -- a sandbox-first model is viable only where the local regulator permits deferred verification before live transactions, and a front-loaded model is close to mandatory where it doesn't. V1 for a new entrant should default to the most permissive sequencing its specific regulatory environment allows, offering sandbox testing with mock transactions immediately and gating real KYC only before real money moves, since that maximizes developer momentum without violating compliance. The risk is treating a regulatory floor as a product choice, either over-complying and losing developers unnecessarily or under-complying and creating real compliance and fraud risk; this connects back to each company's mission -- optimizing time-to-first-integration wherever the law allows it, while staying a compliant, trustworthy rail within whatever regulatory reality the entrant actually operates in.

pitfalls: Treating Razorpay's heavier upfront KYC as simply worse UX, without recognizing it's substantially driven by direct RBI regulatory obligation, not a design preference
Recommending a new entrant copy Stripe's deferred-KYC model without first checking whether its target market's regulator permits that sequencing

cases.title: Why Figma and Adobe diverged on real-time collaboration and file ownership
cases.prompt: Figma was built browser-first with real-time multiplayer editing and cloud-hosted files from the start; Adobe's design tools grew up as desktop-native applications with locally-owned files, later adding cloud sync and co-editing on top. Why might these two design-software companies have made such different foundational bets on collaboration and file ownership, and which approach would you choose for a new design tool built today?
context: Figma launched in 2016 as a browser-based design tool with real-time multiplayer editing, including multiple cursors and live co-editing, built into its core architecture from the start.

Adobe's flagship design tools, including Photoshop and Illustrator, originated as desktop-native applications with locally-saved files, later adding Creative Cloud sync and, in tools like Adobe XD, co-editing features.

Adobe announced an agreement to acquire Figma for roughly $20 billion in 2022; the two companies called off the deal in December 2023 after facing regulatory opposition from antitrust authorities in the UK and EU.
assumptions: assumed: comparing the two companies' foundational architecture choices as originally built, not every collaboration feature either has added since
assumed: the interviewer wants a recommendation for a new design tool being architected today
followUps: How would your recommendation change for a tool aimed specifically at print or photography professionals rather than product teams?
What's the biggest technical risk of a browser-based, cloud-native architecture for very large, complex files?
How does the blocked Adobe-Figma acquisition change how you'd think about competing in this space today?

stages.walkthrough: I'll compare the two companies' foundational architecture choices as originally built, not every collaboration feature either has added since, and assume the interviewer wants a recommendation for a new design tool being architected today. My plan: connect each company's mission to its architecture choice, segment the users each architecture serves, identify the specific problem each solves, then recommend an approach for a new tool.

Figma's mission from day one was making design a team sport -- collaboration that felt as live and shared as a real-time document, built for a world where product teams, not lone designers, needed to co-create and hand off work fluidly, which required a browser-first, cloud-native architecture since real-time multiplayer over locally-owned files isn't practically achievable. Adobe's design tools were built in an earlier era where the mission was empowering a single skilled creative professional with deep, offline-capable creative control -- Photoshop and Illustrator's architecture reflects that individual-craftsperson origin, with collaboration retrofitted onto a foundation designed for one person's file, not built for it from the start.

Figma's core segment is cross-functional product teams -- designers, PMs, engineers -- who need to view, comment on, and sometimes edit the same file simultaneously as part of a fast iteration loop, where file ownership by one person would be an active obstacle. Adobe's core segment historically has been individual creative professionals, such as photographers, illustrators, and print designers, producing polished, often offline deliverables where a single owner controlling a file's state is a feature, and heavy local processing power matters more than live multiplayer.

For Figma's product-team persona, the journey moment is a design review where three people need to look at and annotate the same frame at the same time without emailing files back and forth -- the problem is that file-based, single-owner workflows make simultaneous collaboration structurally impossible, not just inconvenient. For Adobe's creative-professional persona, the journey moment is deep, focused, often offline editing work where local file ownership and full control over versioning matters more than real-time visibility to others -- their problem historically wasn't collaboration friction, it was ensuring uninterrupted creative control over a complex, resource-intensive file.

For a new design tool built today, the architecture choice should follow the primary use case: cloud-native multiplayer if the product's core value is cross-functional team collaboration, or local-first with optional cloud sync if the core value is deep, offline-capable, single-owner craftsmanship. Given how much modern product work has shifted toward cross-functional collaboration as the default expectation, I'd default a new general-purpose design tool to cloud-native multiplayer, treating offline access as a secondary capability layered on top rather than the foundation; the key risk is that browser-based architecture can struggle with very large, complex files that push against browser performance limits, a real weakness against desktop-native tools for heavy creative work. This choice serves a mission of making design a continuously shared, team-visible process rather than a series of handoffs.

pitfalls: Declaring cloud-native multiplayer the objectively modern and therefore correct choice for every design tool, ignoring that heavy creative work still benefits from local processing power and single-owner control
Treating the Adobe-Figma acquisition attempt as proof one architecture won, when the deal was blocked by antitrust regulators, not settled by the market

cases.title: Designing Google Maps for two-wheeler gig delivery riders in Indian cities
cases.prompt: Design an improved navigation experience within Google Maps for gig delivery riders on two-wheelers in dense Indian cities, who navigate narrow lanes, mixed traffic, and time-pressured deliveries all day.
context: Google Maps launched a dedicated 'two-wheeler mode' for India in 2018, offering routes that account for narrow lanes and shortcuts usable by motorbikes and scooters but not cars.
India's food and grocery delivery gig economy relies heavily on two-wheeler riders navigating dense urban traffic for time-sensitive deliveries.
Two-wheeler mode in Google Maps is available as a distinct vehicle-type option alongside driving, walking, and transit modes.
assumptions: assumed: designing specifically for riders doing 20-plus deliveries a day in a single dense metro, not occasional personal two-wheeler use
assumed: riders primarily navigate one-handed via a phone mount while riding, with limited attention available for reading a screen
followUps: How would your design change for a rider in a city where two-wheeler mode data, like narrow-lane routing, is less mature?
What's the tradeoff between the fastest route and the safest route for a time-pressured rider, and how would you handle it?
How would you know if your changes were actually saving riders time versus just feeling faster?

stages.walkthrough: I'll scope this to riders doing many deliveries a day in a single dense Indian metro on a phone-mounted device, where attention available for the screen is minimal and one-handed control matters. My plan: connect this to Google Maps' broader mission, segment the ecosystem of people using two-wheeler mode, define this rider persona behaviourally, map their delivery-day journey to find the real problem, then propose a solution.

Google Maps' mission is to help anyone get anywhere accurately and confidently, and two-wheeler mode already reflects the recognition that a car-centric route model fails a huge share of Indian commuters. For gig delivery riders specifically, the deeper need isn't just getting from A to B -- it's completing as many trips as possible, safely, within a tightly time-boxed day, which reframes navigation from a single-trip tool into something closer to a daily working tool. This matters strategically because Google Maps already has the richest lane-level and traffic data in the market, a strength no delivery-specific app can independently replicate.

The ecosystem includes riders, the restaurants or stores they pick up from, the customers receiving deliveries, and the delivery platforms whose own in-app maps often just wrap Google Maps data. Within riders, I'd segment behaviourally: riders doing back-to-back deliveries in a small, memorized radius who rarely need turn-by-turn at all, riders who get long-distance or unfamiliar-area orders occasionally and need full navigation support, and new riders in their first weeks who need navigation for nearly every trip since they haven't built area knowledge yet. These are mutually exclusive because an experienced local rider's problem is confirming a shortcut exists, while a new rider's problem is having no mental map at all -- prioritizing new riders makes sense since they're the most underserved and every rider passes through this stage.

Mapping a new rider's day: they accept an order, navigate to an unfamiliar pickup point that's often inside a market or gully with no clean address, then navigate again to a delivery point that might be an apartment gate rather than the building itself, then repeat immediately with a new pickup elsewhere. The sharpest problem isn't route-finding on main roads, which two-wheeler mode already handles reasonably well -- it's the last hundred meters at both ends, where addresses are ambiguous and a rider loses minutes circling a location that a car-centric address system was never built to pinpoint. This is a real problem because it's frequent, occurring at every single delivery, and severe, since minutes lost per stop compound across a full day's targets, directly undercutting the mission of getting a time-pressured worker exactly where they need to be with confidence.

Three directions: a rider-specific last-approach view showing a zoomed, landmark-annotated path to the exact drop point rather than a street-level pin, sourced from prior riders' successful arrival points at the same address; a lightweight voice-first mode reading out only critical turns and landmark cues to minimize screen glances while riding; and a crowdsourced delivery-entry-point layer where riders and platforms jointly correct ambiguous addresses over time. On an impact x effort grid, the last-approach view wins for V1: it directly targets the highest-frequency, highest-severity pain point, and it can bootstrap off delivery-platform data through partnership rather than requiring a new crowdsourcing system from zero. The key risk is stale or wrong crowdsourced arrival points misleading a rider worse than no data at all, mitigated by only surfacing a corrected pin once enough independent riders have confirmed the same arrival point. This serves the mission of confident navigation by closing the exact gap where today's address systems fail hardest.

pitfalls: Focusing on faster main-road routing when the real time loss for delivery riders is concentrated in the ambiguous final approach at each stop
Designing a rich visual interface that assumes more screen attention than a rider actually has while moving through traffic

cases.title: Designing PhonePe's first payment experience for Tier-2/3 India's first-time digital-payment users
cases.prompt: Design the first-payment experience within PhonePe for someone in Tier-2 or Tier-3 India who has a smartphone and a bank account but has never made a digital payment before, and is nervous about doing it wrong.
context: PhonePe launched in 2015 and became one of India's largest UPI (Unified Payments Interface) apps by transaction volume, per India's National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) published data.
UPI enables instant bank-to-bank transfers in India using a mobile app, without needing to share bank account or card details directly with a merchant.
PhonePe has expanded distribution beyond metro India into smaller towns, including through offline merchant QR-code partnerships.
assumptions: assumed: this user has a bank account linked to their phone number, a UPI prerequisite, but has never completed a real digital transaction
assumed: fear of an irreversible mistake, such as sending money to the wrong person or amount, is the dominant emotional barrier for this segment, more than not understanding what UPI is conceptually
followUps: How would your design change for a user who has used digital payments before but only via a bank's own app, not a UPI app like PhonePe?
What's the risk of over-explaining every step to a segment that might actually just want to get the payment done quickly once they trust it?
How would you measure whether a first-timer's anxiety actually decreased, not just whether they completed the payment?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume this user has a linked bank account but has never completed a real UPI transaction, and that fear of an irreversible mistake, not conceptual confusion about what UPI is, is their dominant barrier. My plan: connect this to PhonePe's mission, segment the people in this journey, define this persona's behavioural profile, map their first-payment journey to find the real problem, then propose a solution.

PhonePe's mission is making digital payments the default way anyone in India moves money, and its growth beyond metro India into smaller towns means its next wave of users increasingly includes people for whom a digital transaction is a genuinely novel, slightly frightening act rather than a routine one. The deeper human need for this segment isn't payment speed -- it's trust that money won't disappear into an app they don't fully understand, which reframes the product problem from making payments fast to making a first payment feel safe enough to attempt. PhonePe's existing scale and offline merchant QR presence is a real strength here, since a first-timer is more likely to trust an app they've already seen a shopkeeper use successfully.

The ecosystem includes the payer, the receiving merchant or individual, PhonePe itself, and the banks whose rails PhonePe rides on. Within first-time users, I'd segment behaviourally rather than by age or income: confident-but-untested users who understand the concept from watching others but haven't personally tried it, anxious-and-untested users who both lack experience and actively fear making an irreversible error, and coached users who have someone nearby actively walking them through their very first transaction. These are mutually exclusive in what they need: the confident group mainly needs a low-friction first success, while the anxious group needs active reassurance before they'll even attempt the tap; I'd prioritize the anxious-and-untested segment since they're both large and the most underserved by a generic payment flow built for people who already trust the system.

Mapping this persona's journey: they open PhonePe at a shop counter with a queue behind them, see a QR code and an amount field, and freeze at the moment of typing the amount and hitting confirm, because they have no felt sense of what happens if they mistype a digit or the wrong recipient. The problem isn't discovering how to scan a QR code, which is a relatively simple, learnable action -- it's the confirm-and-send moment itself, where an irreversible action with real money attached meets zero prior lived experience of it going right. This is a real problem because it's severe, since a mistaken transfer can be genuinely hard to reverse, and it directly blocks PhonePe's mission: an app that isn't trusted at the exact moment of commitment will never become anyone's default.

Three directions: a one-time, skippable guided-first-payment overlay that narrates each step in plain language the first time only, then disappears for all subsequent payments; a pre-confirm summary screen showing the recipient's verified name, not just a UPI ID, alongside the amount and a single large confirm action, reducing the chance of an unnoticed error at the exact commit moment; and a prominent payment-sent confirmation with the recipient's verified name, closing the loop so the user leaves with proof it worked rather than lingering doubt. On an impact x effort grid, the pre-confirm summary screen wins for V1: it's low effort since much of this data already exists in the transaction, and it directly targets the highest-anxiety moment rather than general education the user may not read anyway. The key risk is that added friction could annoy repeat users; mitigation is showing the enhanced summary prominently only for a user's first several transactions, then quietly stepping back once behaviour shows familiarity. This serves the mission of becoming India's default payment method by making the very first use of it feel safe enough to repeat.

pitfalls: Assuming this segment's barrier is understanding UPI conceptually, when the sharper barrier is the felt risk of an irreversible mistake at the moment of confirming
Adding permanent, heavy explanatory UI that annoys the same user once they've become a confident repeat payer

cases.title: Designing Amazon's shopping experience for first-time online shoppers in Tier-2/3 India
cases.prompt: Design an improved shopping experience within the Amazon app for someone in Tier-2 or Tier-3 India buying something online for the very first time, who is more comfortable in a regional language than in English.
context: Amazon India has added support for multiple Indian regional languages within its shopping app, alongside its default English and Hindi interfaces.
Amazon has operated 'Amazon Easy' physical assisted-shopping points in smaller Indian towns, where a local store representative helps a customer place their first order.
Amazon India's addressable market extends well beyond metro cities into smaller towns with lower prior exposure to online shopping.
assumptions: assumed: this user owns a smartphone and has some prior comfort with apps generally, such as messaging apps, but has never completed an online purchase
assumed: distrust of paying before receiving the item, more than language alone, is a major reason this segment hasn't shopped online before
followUps: How would your design differ for a user who has cash-on-delivery available versus one who doesn't?
What's the risk of translating the interface into a regional language but leaving product reviews and descriptions in English?
How would you decide which regional languages to prioritize first?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume this user owns a smartphone, has general app familiarity, but has never completed an online purchase, and that distrust of paying before receiving an item, not language alone, is a major reason they haven't shopped online yet. My plan: connect this to Amazon's mission, segment the people relevant to a first purchase, define this persona behaviourally, map their first-purchase journey, then propose a solution.

Amazon's mission is to be Earth's most customer-centric company, offering the widest selection at low prices with reliable delivery, a promise that only fully lands once someone actually experiences it, which is exactly the barrier for a population that has never completed the loop of ordering, paying, and receiving. Amazon India's investment in regional-language support and physical assisted-shopping points signals recognition that reach into smaller towns requires more than translating English UI text; it requires closing a trust gap that metro, already-converted shoppers don't have. This matters strategically because India's next major wave of e-commerce growth is understood to come disproportionately from exactly this under-penetrated segment.

The ecosystem includes the buyer, the seller, often a third-party marketplace seller on Amazon, the delivery courier, and Amazon itself. Within first-time Tier-2/3 shoppers, I'd segment behaviourally: language-comfortable browsers who understand English reasonably well but still hesitate to commit to a purchase, regional-language-first users who struggle to evaluate a product description or review written only in English, and trust-blocked users for whom the core hesitation isn't language at all but fear of paying without seeing the item first. I'd prioritize the trust-blocked segment: it's likely the largest reach group among true first-timers, and it's the most underserved since most product-page improvements to date focus on translation and browsing rather than the deeper payment-trust barrier.

Mapping the trust-blocked persona's journey: they browse and find something they want, reach the payment step, and stall, not because the product page is unclear, but because they have no prior lived experience that paying online and having the item arrive later actually works as promised. The problem isn't product discovery -- it's that the single largest source of reassurance available, someone they trust telling them it works, is entirely absent from a first-time solo online purchase, unlike an in-person shop where a shopkeeper's presence itself is reassuring. This is a real problem because it's the single highest-severity blocker in the entire funnel: everything upstream can go perfectly and the purchase still won't complete, directly undermining Amazon's mission of being trusted with a customer's very first purchase.

Three directions: surface cash-on-delivery prominently as the default payment option for first-time buyers in under-penetrated pin codes, removing the pay-before-trust problem entirely for a first purchase; show a lightweight, localized delivery-explainer with real delivery-tracking visuals the first time a first-timer reaches checkout; and surface reviews and ratings from other buyers in the same city or region prominently, so trust comes from a recognizable local signal rather than an anonymous aggregate. On an impact x effort grid, defaulting to cash-on-delivery for this segment wins for V1: it's low build effort since the payment option already exists, and it directly removes the highest-severity blocker rather than trying to build trust in prepayment through messaging alone. The key risk is COD's higher return and non-pickup rates hurting unit economics; mitigation is treating it as a deliberate, temporary acquisition cost for a user's first one or two orders, then nudging toward prepayment once a successful delivery has built real trust. This serves Amazon's mission by making the very first purchase completable at all, the precondition for every purchase after it.

pitfalls: Treating regional-language translation alone as sufficient, when the deeper barrier for many first-timers is trust in the pay-then-receive model, not comprehension
Pushing prepayment options to reduce COD costs before a first-time user has any lived experience that the delivery promise is real

cases.title: Designing Airtel Payments Bank for underbanked, low-literacy rural users
cases.prompt: Design a core banking experience within Airtel Payments Bank for a rural, low-literacy user who has never held a formal bank account and relies on a local Airtel retail point as their primary access to banking.
context: Airtel Payments Bank launched in 2017 as one of India's first payments banks, a category permitted to accept deposits and enable payments but not issue loans directly.
Airtel Payments Bank operates largely through Airtel's existing retail network of local recharge and recharge-point shops, which double as banking correspondent points in many areas.
Payments banks in India were created partly to extend basic banking access to populations that traditional bank branches had not reached, particularly in rural areas.
assumptions: assumed: this user cannot confidently read most Hindi or English text on a screen and relies on a trusted local retail-point operator to complete most transactions on their behalf
assumed: the user's core need is depositing and withdrawing small amounts of cash reliably, not investment or credit products
followUps: How would your design change if this user had a basic smartphone versus only a feature phone?
What's the risk of designing a self-service app for a segment that currently relies on a trusted human intermediary for every transaction?
How would you measure trust in this segment, given they may not complain even when something goes wrong?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume this user cannot confidently read most on-screen text, relies on a trusted local retail-point operator for transactions today, and mainly needs reliable small-amount cash deposits and withdrawals rather than credit or investment products. My plan: connect this to Airtel Payments Bank's mission, segment the ecosystem around this user, define this persona behaviourally, map their banking journey to find the real problem, then propose a solution.

Airtel Payments Bank's mission is extending basic banking access to people traditional branch banking has never reached, using Airtel's existing retail footprint as the delivery mechanism rather than building new branches. The deeper human need for this segment isn't a banking app with more features -- it's the basic confidence that money deposited with a local retail point is safe, recorded correctly, and retrievable on demand, a level of trust that formal banking has historically failed to earn from this population. This plays directly to Airtel's strength: an already-trusted local retail presence in places a traditional bank branch has never existed.

The ecosystem includes the account holder, the local retail-point operator who often acts as the human interface for a transaction, and Airtel Payments Bank itself. Within underbanked rural users, I'd segment behaviourally: fully intermediary-dependent users who complete every transaction through the retail-point operator and never touch the app themselves, partially self-sufficient users who can handle a simple deposit or balance check alone but still rely on the operator for anything unfamiliar, and emerging self-service users, often younger family members, who could operate the app directly if it were designed for their literacy level. I'd prioritize the fully intermediary-dependent segment since it's likely the largest and most underserved, with most banking-app design assuming a self-service user and leaving this group's actual experience entirely undesigned.

Mapping this persona's journey: they walk to the local retail point with cash to deposit or a need to withdraw, hand over their details verbally, and rely entirely on the operator correctly entering the transaction and communicating back an accurate confirmation. The problem isn't the underlying banking rails, which function correctly -- it's that this user has no independent way to verify a transaction happened correctly, since they can't read a confirmation SMS or app screen themselves, leaving them structurally dependent on the operator's honesty and accuracy with no personal fallback. This is a real problem because it's severe, since an error or dishonest operator could mean lost savings with no way for the user to detect or contest it, and it directly undermines the mission: a banking system this population can't independently verify isn't meaningfully more trustworthy than having no formal bank account at all.

Three directions: a mandatory, simple audio confirmation call or voice message in the user's language after every transaction, independent of the retail-point operator's own confirmation, giving the user a channel the operator doesn't control; a physical, printed passbook-style receipt with large numerals and icons rather than dense text, handed over at every transaction as a tangible record; and a periodic, automated voice-call balance check the user can trigger by giving a missed call to a known number. On an impact x effort grid, the automated post-transaction voice confirmation wins for V1: it directly closes the highest-severity gap of no independent verification at relatively low technical cost, since it reuses existing telephony infrastructure Airtel already operates at scale. The key risk is the user not recognizing or trusting an automated call versus a human one; mitigation is designing the message to sound clearly official and piloting it with visible retail-point staff endorsement to build initial trust. This serves the mission of real banking access by giving this user, for the first time, a way to verify their own money independent of any single human intermediary.

pitfalls: Designing a more feature-rich self-service app when this segment's core unmet need is independent verification of a transaction, not more app functionality
Assuming literacy is the only barrier and missing that structural dependency on a single human intermediary is the deeper trust problem

cases.title: Designing Facebook Lite for users on unreliable 2G/3G networks and low-end devices
cases.prompt: Design an improved core experience within Facebook Lite for users in emerging markets on intermittent 2G or 3G networks and older, storage-constrained Android devices.
context: Facebook launched Facebook Lite in 2015, a lightweight Android app built with a small install size and reduced data usage, targeting users on slower networks and lower-end devices.
Facebook Lite was designed to work on 2G networks and devices with limited internal storage, as a lighter alternative to the main Facebook app.
A substantial share of global Facebook users access the platform primarily through mobile networks in regions where high-speed, reliable connectivity is not guaranteed.
assumptions: assumed: this user's connection frequently drops mid-session or loads slowly enough that waiting for content is a routine part of their experience
assumed: available device storage is a real constraint, meaning every megabyte the app or its cached content consumes competes directly with other apps and photos
followUps: How would your design change for a user who has a good device but is on a capped, expensive data plan versus one with an old device but unlimited data?
What's the risk of stripping out too much visual richness in the name of lightness?
How would you measure success for this segment differently than for users on fast, unlimited connections?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume this user's connection routinely drops or loads slowly enough that waiting is a normal part of their experience, and that device storage is a real, active constraint competing with their other apps and photos. My plan: connect this to Facebook's mission, segment the ecosystem relevant to this experience, define this persona behaviourally, map their session journey to find the real problem, then propose a solution.

Facebook's stated mission is giving people the power to build community and connect the world, a mission that only holds if the product actually works for the large share of the world's population on unreliable networks and older devices, not just those with fast connections and current-generation phones. The deeper need for this segment isn't a lighter version of the same features -- it's a version of connection that survives the real conditions of their network and device, since a feed that fails to load or a device that runs out of space to install the app defeats the mission entirely for them. Facebook Lite's existence already reflects this recognition, making the ongoing question how to keep pushing that lightness further as network and device conditions in target markets evolve.

The ecosystem includes the user, the friends and pages they connect with who may be on faster connections posting richer content, and Facebook's ad business, which depends on this segment staying engaged enough to see and interact with ads. Within Lite's users, I'd segment behaviourally: intermittent-connection users whose network drops mid-session unpredictably, storage-constrained users who actively delete apps and content to make room and treat every megabyte as a tradeoff, and cost-conscious users on metered data plans who consciously limit how much they scroll to control their data spend. I'd prioritize the intermittent-connection segment since a failed or frozen session is the most severe possible failure -- it doesn't just slow the experience, it can break it entirely mid-use.

Mapping the intermittent-connection persona's journey: they open the app, start scrolling the feed, and their connection drops mid-load, leaving a half-rendered post, a spinning loader, or in the worst case an app that appears frozen with no clear signal of what's happening or what to do next. The problem isn't that content loads slowly -- users on this segment have already adapted to that -- it's the ambiguity of a failed or interrupted load: there's no clear distinction between still-loading and failed, leaving the user unsure whether to wait, retry, or give up. This is a real problem because it's frequent, with network drops a routine occurrence for this segment, and it directly threatens the mission: connection breaks down exactly at the moment a session interruption looks indistinguishable from the app simply not working.

Three directions: explicit, distinguishable connection-state messaging that clearly separates still-loading from connection-lost-tap-to-retry rather than an ambiguous spinner in both cases; aggressive local caching of the most recently loaded feed content so a dropped connection still leaves something usable on screen; and a background retry queue for actions taken while offline, such as likes and comments, that silently completes once connectivity returns. On an impact x effort grid, explicit connection-state messaging wins for V1: it's low effort relative to caching infrastructure, and it directly resolves the highest-frequency source of user confusion without requiring new backend work. The key risk is that distinguishing loading from failed reliably on a genuinely unstable connection is itself a hard technical problem, since a slow load and a failed one can look identical for several seconds; mitigation is a conservative timeout before declaring failure, tuned to observed network conditions in target markets rather than a generic global default. This serves the mission by making the app trustworthy under real conditions, not just ideal ones.

pitfalls: Optimizing purely for load speed when the sharper problem for this segment is the ambiguity of a failed versus still-loading state
Assuming a single generic timeout or caching strategy works globally, when actual network conditions vary significantly by target market

cases.title: Extending Be My Eyes for blind and low-vision users beyond one-off visual assistance calls
cases.prompt: Be My Eyes connects blind and low-vision users with sighted volunteers, and more recently an AI assistant, for live visual help. Design an improvement to the experience for a blind user who wants ongoing, everyday visual assistance, not just occasional one-off help.
context: Be My Eyes launched in 2015 as an app connecting blind and low-vision users with sighted volunteers via live video call for real-time visual assistance.
In 2023, Be My Eyes partnered with OpenAI to add 'Virtual Volunteer,' an AI-powered feature using GPT-4 with vision to describe images and answer visual questions without needing a human volunteer.
Be My Eyes' core original use case is a user pointing their phone camera at something, such as a label, document, or obstacle, and describing what they need help identifying.
assumptions: assumed: this user relies on the app multiple times per day for small, routine visual tasks, not just occasional unusual situations
assumed: a mix of AI and human-volunteer help is available, and the choice between them for a given task matters to the user
followUps: How would your design change for a task where getting the answer wrong has real consequences, like reading a medication label, versus a low-stakes one, like describing a photo?
What's the risk of over-relying on AI answers for tasks where a human volunteer would catch something the AI misses?
How would you know if frequent users are actually building more independence over time, versus growing more dependent on the app for everything?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume this user relies on the app multiple times a day for small, routine visual tasks rather than occasional unusual situations, and that they have a real choice between AI and human-volunteer help for a given task. My plan: connect this to Be My Eyes' mission, segment the people and systems involved, define this frequent-user persona behaviourally, map their daily journey to find the real problem, then propose a solution.

Be My Eyes' mission is bringing sight to those who don't have it, originally through human volunteers and now increasingly through AI as well -- the deeper human need it serves is independence in everyday tasks that sighted people take for granted, from reading a label to identifying an obstacle. For a frequent user, the product's value isn't in any single call, it's in whether it reliably removes small daily friction points enough that the world feels navigable without needing to ask a family member for help constantly. Be My Eyes' unique strength is having pioneered both the human-volunteer network and, more recently, a credible AI alternative, giving it flexibility competitors relying on only one of those two options don't have.

The ecosystem includes the blind or low-vision user, the sighted volunteers who donate their time, the AI system now available as an alternative, and Be My Eyes itself balancing volunteer capacity against AI cost. Within frequent users, I'd segment behaviourally by task stakes: low-stakes routine tasks like identifying an item's color, where a quick, always-available answer matters more than certainty; higher-stakes tasks like reading a medication label, where accuracy matters more than speed; and situationally complex tasks like navigating an unfamiliar space, which may need a real-time, back-and-forth human conversation an AI single-shot answer can't fully replace. I'd prioritize the higher-stakes task segment, since it's where a wrong answer causes real harm and where the choice between AI and human matters most.

Mapping the higher-stakes persona's journey: they need to confirm what a medication label says before taking a dose, open the app, and have to decide in the moment whether to trust a fast AI description or wait for a human volunteer to become available, without a clear, evidence-based signal for which is more reliable for this specific kind of task. The problem isn't availability of help in general -- both channels are generally accessible -- it's that the user currently has no reliable guidance on which channel to trust for a given stakes level, forcing a judgment call they're not well positioned to make correctly every time. This is a real problem because it's severe, since a misread medication label has real health consequences, and it's exactly the kind of moment where the mission of enabling independent daily living is most at stake.

Three directions: task-type prompts at the start of a request that route higher-stakes categories, such as medication and expiry dates, toward human volunteers by default, with AI reserved for lower-stakes tasks; a visible, per-response confidence indicator from the AI, prompting an automatic offer to escalate to a human volunteer whenever confidence is low; and an opt-in personal history of past requests and their outcomes, letting a frequent user learn over time which task types they've personally found the AI reliable for. On an impact x effort grid, routing higher-stakes categories to human volunteers by default is the strongest V1: it directly targets the highest-severity failure mode with a relatively simple rule-based routing change, rather than requiring new confidence-calibration infrastructure from the AI provider. The key risk is under-supply of volunteers if high-stakes routing increases human-call volume beyond available capacity; mitigation is being transparent with the user about expected wait time and offering the AI answer as an immediate, clearly-labeled interim option while a human is found, not as a forced substitute. This serves the mission by making sure the moments that matter most for real independence get the most reliable channel available.

pitfalls: Treating AI and human-volunteer help as interchangeable for every task type, when stakes should determine which channel is offered by default
Optimizing for response speed across the board, when for high-stakes tasks the user's real priority is accuracy over speed

cases.title: Designing Coursera for students learning through intermittent, low-bandwidth connectivity
cases.prompt: Design an improved learning experience within Coursera for students who study primarily on mobile devices with intermittent, low-bandwidth connectivity, and cannot rely on a stable connection through an entire course.
context: Coursera's mobile app supports downloading course videos for offline viewing, allowing learners to watch lectures without an active internet connection.

Coursera partners with universities and companies to offer online courses, certificates, and degrees to a global learner base that includes many students in regions with less reliable internet infrastructure.
Coursera courses typically combine video lectures, reading materials, quizzes, and peer- or auto-graded assignments within a structured weekly schedule.
assumptions: assumed: this student's connection is reliable enough for occasional bulk downloads, such as overnight on Wi-Fi at a shared access point, but not for sustained streaming or real-time interaction during study sessions
assumed: the student is working through a structured, multi-week course rather than browsing content casually
followUps: How would your design change for a student who has no reliable Wi-Fi access at all, only intermittent mobile data?
What's the risk of letting a student download an entire course upfront if their device has limited storage?
How would quizzes and graded assignments need to work differently for a student who's frequently offline?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume this student's connection supports occasional bulk downloads, such as overnight at a shared Wi-Fi access point, but not sustained streaming or real-time interaction during actual study sessions, and that they're working through a structured, multi-week course rather than browsing casually. My plan: connect this to Coursera's mission, segment the ecosystem around this learner, define this persona behaviourally, map their weekly study journey to find the real problem, then propose a solution.

Coursera's mission is providing universal access to world-class learning, a promise that depends entirely on the product working for students without reliable, sustained connectivity, not just those with always-on broadband. The deeper need for this segment isn't just watching video offline, which the app already supports -- it's completing an entire structured course, including the interactive and graded parts, despite connectivity that comes and goes unpredictably across the weeks a course runs. This connects directly to Coursera's competitive position: its scale and university partnerships matter most if the platform can actually deliver a complete learning outcome to under-connected learners, not just video content.

The ecosystem includes the student, the course instructor and teaching staff, peer learners in the same cohort, relevant for peer-graded work, and Coursera's own completion and certification systems. Within low-connectivity students, I'd segment behaviourally: download-and-batch learners who plan ahead, downloading a week's content at once during a rare good-connectivity window, opportunistic learners who grab connectivity in short unpredictable bursts, and deadline-anxious learners who worry connectivity gaps will cause them to miss a graded deadline regardless of effort. I'd prioritize the deadline-anxious segment since missing a graded deadline due to connectivity, not lack of effort or understanding, is the most severe possible outcome for this group, and it's currently unaddressed by an offline-video feature alone.

Mapping the deadline-anxious persona's journey: they download course videos during a rare good-connectivity window, study offline over several days, then reach a quiz or assignment that requires submitting online, timed against a fixed deadline they can't fully control their access around. The problem isn't the learning content itself, which offline video already serves reasonably well -- it's that the graded, interactive parts of the course still assume a connection at the exact moment the student happens to have it, creating real risk of losing course progress or a certificate through no fault of their understanding. This is a real problem because it's severe, since a missed deadline can mean failing a course a student has genuinely mastered, and it undermines the mission most sharply for exactly the students universal access is meant to reach.

Three directions: offline-capable quizzes that can be completed without a connection and sync automatically once one becomes available, timestamped at actual completion rather than sync time; a connectivity-aware deadline model that gives documented low-connectivity learners a slightly extended submission window, verified through their own download-and-sync activity pattern rather than a manual appeal process; and a pre-download full-week package that bundles video, readings, and the quiz itself into one offline-capable unit.
